titre: Germany Puts Two Articles Out of Parliament's Reach
accroche: In 1949, the German Basic Law forbids revising certain principles, even by a two-thirds majority: a response to the fall of Weimar.
contenu_vulgarise:
## What 1933 showed

On March 23, 1933, the Reichstag passes the Enabling Act (*Ermächtigungsgesetz*) by 444 votes to 94: the two-thirds majority required by the Weimar Constitution for any revision. The text, which takes effect the next day, authorizes Hitler's government to legislate alone, including by deviating from the Constitution itself. The procedure scrupulously respects the forms the Weimar Constitution provided for its own revision: that is precisely what allows it to hollow out its guarantees.

## A clause that forbids going back on oneself

In 1949, the Parliamentary Council tasked with writing the Basic Law of the new Federal Republic of Germany draws a direct consequence from that episode. It adopts the text on May 8, 1949, by 53 votes to 12, before it is promulgated on May 23. Article 79, paragraph 3, provides that any revision affecting the federal organization of the country, the participation of the Länder in legislation, or the principles set out in Articles 1 and 20 is “inadmissible”: whatever majority is assembled to vote for it.

Article 1 establishes the inviolability of human dignity; Article 20 sets out the principles of a federal, democratic, and social state, and recognizes a right of resistance as a last resort. Neither can therefore be amended through the regular procedure, not even by the two-thirds majority of the Bundestag and the Bundesrat that Article 79 nonetheless requires for any other revision. The Basic Law thus protects itself against its own amendment mechanism.

## A displacement of the problem, not a solution

Most constitutional revision clauses set a majority threshold but exclude no content: clearing the threshold is enough to change everything. Article 79, paragraph 3, does the opposite, and that is what earns it its nickname, the *Ewigkeitsklausel*, the “eternity clause”: certain contents remain out of reach, however many votes are assembled.

The device does not eliminate the risk it targets, though; it displaces it. Nothing prevents a determined majority from overthrowing the constitutional order outside the prescribed forms, by force rather than by vote: something no revision clause, however locked down, can prevent. What Article 79, paragraph 3, guarantees is only that one can no longer say, as in 1933, that the procedure was respected.

repere.texte: “Eine Änderung dieses Grundgesetzes, durch welche [...] die in den Artikeln 1 und 20 niedergelegten Grundsätze berührt werden, ist unzulässig”: an amendment to the Basic Law that would affect the principles laid down in Articles 1 and 20 is inadmissible.
repere.source: Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany, May 23, 1949, Article 79, paragraph 3

carte.punch: Germany has put two articles of its Constitution out of reach of any vote.
carte.idee: In 1949, the German Basic Law forbids revising certain principles (human dignity, a federal and democratic state), even by the two-thirds majority required for any other revision, in response to the 1933 Enabling Act, passed within the constitutional forms of the time.

quiz.question: Why does Article 79, paragraph 3, of the German Basic Law forbid revising certain principles, even by a two-thirds majority?
choix: Because those principles were adopted by referendum and can be changed only by referendum
Because in 1933, a law passed within the constitutional forms had been used to hollow out the Weimar Constitution's guarantees
Because the occupying powers of 1949 imposed this clause as a condition of German independence
Because the German Länder opposed any revision of the federal Constitution
quiz.explication: The 1933 Enabling Act respected the two-thirds majority required by the Weimar Constitution in order to open the way to unlimited power: the 1949 clause prevents the same majority from one day being used to undo the fundamental principles of the new Constitution.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does Article 79, paragraph 3, protect from any revision, even by a two-thirds majority?
choix: The federal organization, the participation of the Länder in legislation, and the principles of Articles 1 and 20
The whole Constitution, article by article, without exception
The territorial borders of the Federal Republic
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text cites Article 79, paragraph 3: any revision affecting the federal organization, the participation of the Länder, or the principles of Articles 1 and 20 is inadmissible.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the two articles protected by the eternity clause respectively establish?
choix: Article 1 organizes elections, Article 20 creates the Constitutional Court
Article 1 protects human dignity, Article 20 sets out the principles of a federal and democratic state
Article 1 sets the capital, Article 20 the official language
Article 1 creates the Bundestag, Article 20 the Bundesrat
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that Article 1 establishes the inviolability of human dignity, and that Article 20 sets out the principles of a federal, democratic, and social state.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Article 79, paragraph 3, actually guarantee against an overthrow of the constitutional order by force?
choix: It completely prevents a coup from ever overthrowing the Constitution
It guarantees only that one can no longer say the procedure was respected, as in 1933
It obliges the army to intervene in case of an attempted coup
It automatically transfers power to the Federal Constitutional Court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text is explicit: the clause cannot prevent an overthrow by force; it guarantees only that one can no longer claim that the procedure was respected, as in 1933.
